newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt markets break rank, end on bullish note.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt markets break rank, end on bullish note.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.35 PCT (PREV 9.35) US 5-YR 5.93 (PREV 5.95)
* NZ debt rallies across curve at Tuesday's close
* Aggressive buying boosts sentiment
* Political developments lurk in background
New Zealand debt markets overcame their earlier apathy on Tuesday afternoon and staged an impressive rally.
The money market led the way, spurred on by a successful treasury bill tender in which NZ$572 million worth of bids were received for only $75 million of 105-day t-bills, which yielded 8.47 percent.

The 90-day bill rate dropped eight basis points to 8.75 percent while the front futures contract climbed six points to 91.58. The rally occurred despite a 17 point fall in the currency's Trade-Weighted Index to 66.88.

"The t-bill tender went off particularly well, so I think that's added to the confidence of the market, and we had a bit of aggressive inter-bank buying in the afternoon session which has taken it lower," one money market dealer said.

"It looks like that's all that's done it," he said, adding that the market had been grinding lower over the last few days as traders anticipated an easing in monetary conditions within the next month or so.
"It doesn't look like much is going to stop it. The only thing that perhaps now stands in the way is a shock political announcement," he said.
New Zealand is currently without a formal government after an inconclusive election on October 12.

The nationalist New Zealand First Party holds the balance of power, and is negotiating separately with both the caretaker National Party government and the centre-left Labour Party over the shape of the next government.
A bond dealer agreed politics could intrude on the market's contentment.
"It's sustainable ignoring the coalition talks," he said of the rally.
The dealer said the market was very bullish in afternoon trade with one party getting very aggressive on the bonds, and samurai issues this week were likely.
"It was concentrated in the mid bonds -- the 98s out to 01s -- which has got the smell of a dual-currency about it.

"But at the same time the currency wasn't being bought, so there must have been a mismatch of currency and bond hedging. The currency might have been done a couple of days ago, or might yet be required to be done," he said.
The 02/00 bond rallied six basis points to 6.87 percent while the three-year government futures contract rallied 11 points to 93.14.
